topics.title: Valued fields and affinoid algebras
topics.description: Read the foundations of complete valued fields, Tate and affinoid algebras, Banach norms, analytic points and rational domains in non-Archimedean geometry.
topics.introduction: Affinoid geometry begins with algebras of convergent functions over a complete valued field. This reading route follows the construction of Tate algebras, bounded seminorms and completed residue fields, then moves to rational domains and the structure sheaf. Chapter 1 treats both strict presentations and arbitrary radii, with attention to the norms used in scalar extension and finite modules. Chapter 2 uses this algebra to construct local analytic geometry and explains the role of completed tensor products in fibres. Reduction in Chapter 3 connects these analytic norms with algebra over the residue field.

topics.title: Berkovich analytic spaces
topics.description: Explore Berkovich spectra and analytic spaces through seminorms, affinoid domains, completed residue fields, analytic fibres, flatness and properness.
topics.introduction: Berkovich points are described by bounded multiplicative seminorms, so an analytic space contains more than the points valued in its ground field. Begin with the spectra and residue fields in Chapter 1. Chapter 2 builds analytic spaces from affinoid pieces and studies domains, morphisms, fibres and local geometric properties. The distinction between an analytic domain, a closed subspace and a scalar extension matters throughout the later differential theory. Chapter 4 provides concrete pictures on the analytic line and on curves, while Chapter 6 explains how finite coordinate data and tropical maps record parts of this geometry.

topics.title: Formal models and reduction
topics.description: A reading route through canonical and graded reduction, formal models, admissible blowups, residual geometry and model metrics on Berkovich spaces.
topics.introduction: Reduction relates non-Archimedean analytic geometry to algebraic geometry over a residue field. Chapter 3 distinguishes canonical reduction, which uses the spectral seminorm, from a chosen formal model and its special fibre. It also introduces graded reduction, admissible blowups and the residual information carried by an analytic germ. The curve chapter uses formal models to describe semistable geometry and skeleta. For line bundles, formal frames give model metrics, whose positivity is studied later through residual degrees and curve tests. Following these chapters together keeps the analytic space, its chosen model and the numerical data of that model in view.

topics.title: Analytic curves and skeleta
topics.description: Find definitions and calculations for Berkovich curves, discs, annuli, semistable skeleta, residual directions, integral slopes and graph potentials.
topics.introduction: Analytic curves make the geometry of non-Archimedean points and reduction particularly explicit. Chapter 4 starts with disc seminorms and the topology of the analytic line, then studies annuli, residual curves, semistable models and slope formulas. Its field hypotheses distinguish the point classification from annulus calculations that work more generally. Chapter 6 compares these skeleta with tropical coordinates and faithful maps. The later chapters on harmonic forms and Chern measures return to metric graphs, where differential complexes, Laplacians and Green kernels can be calculated. This route connects the geometric skeleton with the analytic operations subsequently performed on it.

topics.title: Tropicalization, multiplicities and balancing
topics.description: Read tropicalization through initial degenerations, tropical multiplicities, lattice indices, balancing, analytic moment maps and stable intersections.
topics.introduction: Tropicalization records the valuations of functions, while multiplicities retain geometric information that the underlying polyhedral set alone does not contain. Chapter 5 develops initial degenerations, weights, lattice indices and balancing before turning to analytic moment maps and finite pushforward. Its examples include hypersurface weights, binomial intersections and the role of cancellation at a weighted Gauss point. Chapter 6 explains how these tropical images relate to analytic charts and skeleta. Chapter 15 then uses weighted cycles in polyhedral intersection calculus. This route is useful for following where a tropical weight comes from and how that weight enters integration or an intersection product.

topics.title: Faithful tropicalization and skeletal charts
topics.description: Explore faithful tropicalization, skeletal charts, Gauss sections, tropical fibres, integral-affine coordinates and refinements of analytic moment maps.
topics.introduction: A tropical map can lose information about an analytic space, so the choice of coordinates is part of the geometry. Chapter 6 studies skeleta, Gauss sections, tropical fibres and the conditions under which additional coordinates faithfully describe a compact skeleton. Chapter 5 supplies the accompanying lattice calculations, semistable charts and finite analytic degree arguments. Chapter 4 provides the curve skeleta on which many of these constructions can first be seen. The final link to Chapter 8 follows the passage from moment coordinates to differential forms and integration, where coordinate changes must preserve more than the topology of the tropical image.

topics.title: Chambert–Loir–Ducros differential forms
topics.description: Study Chambert–Loir–Ducros forms through real superforms, tropical charts, positivity cones, compactly supported tests, integration and Stokes formulas.
topics.introduction: The Chambert–Loir–Ducros approach brings a real differential calculus to non-Archimedean analytic spaces using tropical coordinates. Chapter 7 begins with the double complex of superforms and the distinctions between positivity cones. Chapter 8 constructs the original smooth forms from analytic moment maps and develops integration, weights, compactly supported tests and Stokes formulas. Chapter 9 passes to currents acting on these tests. Chapter 18 places this calculus beside delta-forms and harmonic or weakly smooth forms, recording what the comparison maps require. The route separates the local coordinate presentation of a form from the intrinsic object represented by it.

topics.title: Currents, positivity and order zero
topics.description: Find non-Archimedean currents, test-form topologies, positivity cones, order-zero estimates, continuous multipliers and Poincaré–Lelong identities.
topics.introduction: A current is determined by how it acts on a specified space of test forms. Chapter 9 makes that test space explicit and studies order zero, measure coefficients, multiplication by continuous functions and weak convergence. Chapter 7 supplies the positivity cones and domination estimates used in these arguments. Chapter 10 then connects logarithmic singularities, cycle multiplicities and Poincaré–Lelong formulas, with interval and annulus calculations to fix the signs. Chapter 13 applies multiplication and distributional differentiation to continuous Bedford–Taylor products. Reading in this order clarifies which operations are available for a given current and which assumptions are needed for their limits.

topics.title: Plurisubharmonic functions and regularization
topics.description: Read non-Archimedean psh functions, continuous potentials, generated approximation classes, regularized maxima, common domains and model positivity.
topics.introduction: The foundations compare several notions of plurisubharmonicity and the approximation properties attached to them. Chapter 11 introduces continuous potentials and generated classes, discusses changes between the 2012 and 2025 definitions, and tracks the neighbourhood on which an approximating family is defined. Chapter 12 provides regularized maxima, gluing tools and finite barriers. Chapter 19 connects curvewise positivity and model metrics with numerical conditions on residual line bundles. These chapters should be read with the distinction between a current inequality, a curve test and a specified approximation class in mind; each supplies different information for the subsequent Bedford–Taylor construction.

topics.title: Continuous non-Archimedean Bedford–Taylor products
topics.description: A guide to continuous non-Archimedean Bedford–Taylor products, mixed curvature measures, local mass estimates, potential independence and comparison.
topics.introduction: Continuous Bedford–Taylor products combine multiplication of a current by a potential with distributional differentiation. Chapter 13 develops this construction for the admitted potential classes, including mixed products, mass estimates, locality, symmetry and continuity. Chapter 11 supplies the relevant approximation hypotheses, and Chapter 9 supplies the order-zero and multiplication results. Chapter 14 studies the separate question of independence from a chosen potential, using skeletal currents and graph kernels. The comparison and capacity statements in the linked chapter retain their specified continuous domain; this reading route does not identify them with a completed theory for every bounded or unbounded psh function.

topics.title: Delta-forms and tropical intersection
topics.description: Explore Gubler–Künnemann delta-forms, polyhedral currents, stable intersection, analytic quotients, positivity and comparisons with Mihatsch forms.
topics.introduction: Delta-forms combine smooth coefficients with integration over weighted tropical cycles. Chapter 15 begins with delta-preforms and explains how stable intersection enters their product, including balancing, displacement and the independence of a representation. Chapter 16 passes to analytic delta-forms, where the admissible pullbacks and the universal quotient are essential parts of the definition. It also discusses positivity, differential operators and Mihatsch's skeletal construction under its comparison hypotheses. Chapter 18 compares the resulting objects with original and harmonic differential forms. The common thread is the extra geometric structure that makes products possible beyond the smooth calculus.

topics.title: Harmonic coordinates and weakly smooth forms
topics.description: Read harmonic tropicalizations, Gubler–Jell–Rabinoff weakly smooth forms, residual obstructions, graph cohomology and comparisons with CLD forms.
topics.introduction: Logarithms of analytic units do not capture every numerical harmonic function. Chapter 17 explains this through residual line-bundle data and introduces harmonic coordinates and weakly smooth forms. It then studies graph forms, harmonic cohomology and the differential complex on a compact graph. Chapter 18 compares these sheaves with the original smooth calculus and delta-forms, keeping the objects and admissible morphisms separate. Chapter 14 provides a related discussion of harmonic kernels and the gluing of potentials. Together, the chapters show why the choice of differential sheaf affects both local representatives and the global questions one can formulate.

topics.title: Model metrics and semipositivity
topics.description: Study formal and model metrics, residual line bundles, curvewise positivity, numerical nefness, approximation and non-Archimedean semipositivity.
topics.introduction: A formal line bundle determines a metric on the analytic generic fibre through its local frames. Chapter 3 gives this construction and its behaviour under a change of model. Chapter 19 studies the further positivity conditions, relating curve tests and residual degrees to model semipositivity. It also records the hypotheses behind approximation, envelope and variational arguments. Chapter 11 provides the psh and generated approximation classes used in those comparisons. Chapter 20 then follows the metric into its Chern measures. This route keeps numerical properties of a model distinct from analytic curvature conditions until the relevant comparison has been specified.

topics.title: Chern measures and intersection theory
topics.description: Find Chambert–Loir measures, mixed Chern measures, Fubini–Study metrics, intersection degrees, total mass, metric variation and graph Green kernels.
topics.introduction: Chern measures turn the geometry of metrized line bundles into measures on a non-Archimedean analytic space. Chapter 20 begins with residual bundles and model measures, then studies Fubini–Study weights, mixed curvature, total mass and metric variation. It also connects graph Laplacians with intersection matrices and Green kernels. Chapter 19 provides the semipositivity conditions on model metrics, while Chapter 13 supplies continuous mixed products for its admitted potential classes. Chapter 21 treats canonical and toric examples. Read together, these chapters explain how local curvature calculations, degrees on a model and global intersection quantities fit into the same discussion.

topics.title: Canonical and toric metrics
topics.description: Explore canonical metrics, toric convex weights, Monge–Ampère measures, roof functions, equidistribution and the tropical geometry of abelian varieties.
topics.introduction: Chapter 21 brings the metric and measure constructions into canonical and toric settings. It begins with the residual and tropical parts of abelian uniformization, then studies convex toric weights, real Monge–Ampère measures and roof functions. Later sections discuss Tate's limiting construction, canonical heights, equidistribution and the tropical measure argument associated with Bogomolov questions. The chapter also examines boundary mass and the hypotheses of toric comparison formulas. Chapter 20 supplies mixed measures and energy variation, and Chapter 6 supplies the earlier skeletal and tropical language. This route connects concrete convex calculations with the arithmetic uses of non-Archimedean metrics.

topics.title: Non-Archimedean Green objects
topics.description: Read non-Archimedean Green forms and currents, higher-codimension constructions, complete intersections, local heights, test spaces and descent.
topics.introduction: Green objects connect differential equations with algebraic cycles and local intersection pairings. Chapter 22 examines complete-intersection constructions, Bochner–Martinelli and Levine formulas, extension across analytic subsets and the multiplicities in finite-flat comparisons. It distinguishes several categories of Green objects, including the test classes on which their identities are asserted. Chapter 10 supplies the divisor-level Poincaré–Lelong calculation, and Chapter 16 supplies delta-forms. Chapter 23 studies field extension and descent, while Chapter 24 records cohomological questions and remaining comparisons. These links describe the available constructions and their conditions without asserting a general Green-form existence theorem.
